The Government of Vietnam Proposes a Pilot Visa for Remote Workers

Minister of Culture, Sports and Tourism Lam Thi Phuong Thanh presented a draft resolution on special mechanisms and policies for tourism development to the National Assembly. The draft proposes a controlled pilot program for foreigners working remotely in Vietnam. It also includes more flexible visa and residency conditions for medical tourists and individuals coming for long-term treatment, rehabilitation, or relaxation, along with accompanying family members.

The proposal aims to attract higher-spending tourists and strengthen the competitiveness of the tourism industry. The draft includes the expansion of bilateral visa-free regimes for key markets and a more flexible visa policy prioritizing high-income, long-stay, and repeat visitors, as well as conference participants. The government also proposes simplifying the issuance of work permits, visas, and temporary residence for foreign experts and artists involved in tourism projects.

The pilot program for remote workers has not yet been adopted. The Culture and Social Affairs Committee of the National Assembly, while assessing the project, noted that the resolution should not establish specific visa rules for separate groups and called for further clarification on the novelty, features, and boundaries of the proposed special visa policy. Specific rules, fees, and application procedures for the pilot visa have not been established. Remote workers will continue to use the standard electronic visa valid for up to 90 days.

📌 Blind Signing: Why Approving What You Can’t Read Is Dangerous

Main Points
⏺ Your wallet sometimes asks you to sign data it cannot decode
⏺ You see a hash or raw hex instead of clear actions
⏺ This post explains why blind signing is risky and how to avoid it


1⃣ Core Idea — Blind signing means approving a transaction or message without a readable summary of what it actually does.
2⃣ Why It Exists — Some smart contracts are complex, and hardware wallets or apps can’t always parse them, so they show only a hash.
3⃣ Example — You expect to claim a reward, but the hidden payload is a token approval or a transfer of your NFTs to someone else.
4⃣ Risk Surface — Phishing sites rely on this: once you sign, the transaction is valid and usually can’t be reversed.
5⃣ Practical Rule — Keep blind signing off by default, use wallets with transaction simulation, and never sign on a site you reached from a DM or ad.
Final Thoughts

A signature is not a formality — it is your consent. If your wallet can’t tell you what you’re approving, assume the worst and stop.

⚠️ Western Europe’s crypto economy hits $2.08 trillion as stablecoin use surges 

💭 Western Europe’s cryptocurrency economy has reached $2.08 trillion in annual activity, with stablecoin holdings rising 131% even as the region’s largest market, the United Kingdom, recorded a decline. The region was among only three worldwide to record positive growth during the period, alongside Sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America. The UK remained Europe’s largest crypto market, handling $424.5 billion in activity despite an 8% annual contraction, largely attributed to lower decentralized exchange trading.

📌 Germany followed with $288.8 billion, while France recorded $215.8 billion. The Netherlands accounted for $207.8 billion, followed by Spain at $156.1 billion and Switzerland at $132.8 billion. Together, the six countries represented roughly two-thirds of the region’s cryptocurrency activity. Stablecoin holdings in personal wallets across Western Europe rose 131% during the reporting period, compared with global growth of 52%.

🔄 Chainalysis found that the region’s share of worldwide stablecoin balances climbed from 3.4% to 5.1%, with Austria and France recording particularly strong growth. The expansion comes as European financial institutions develop regulated stablecoin products under the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation, or MiCA. Jan-Oliver Sell, CEO of Qivalis, told Chainalysis that regulated euro stablecoins could serve “as the on-chain cash leg for tokenised assets” and support programmable business payments.

Now, in Washington, analysts are openly saying that the scandal has weakened NVIDIA’s ability to block these legislative proposals.
For those seeking to restrict everything, the timing couldn’t be better.

Why does this matter so much? Because open source is the only thing standing between artificial intelligence and a tool of centralized control.

As long as AI remains open, anyone can download a model, study it, modify it, and run it on their own computer. A student in Lagos. A small business in Ohio. Nobody can switch it off. Nobody gets to decide what that machine is allowed to say.
What happens if open source is destroyed?

What’s left are a handful of closed models. Licensed. Tested, approved, and controlled by a federal agency. And when that agency decides what AI is allowed to say, it effectively decides what billions of people will read, learn, and think.

That’s no longer technology. That’s a Ministry of Truth with an API.

And don’t believe for a second that these regulations will hurt the giants.

Nobel Prize-winning economist George Stigler demonstrated that regulation is often captured by the very players it is supposedly designed to restrain. A multimillion-dollar license? The giants can pay for it without blinking. 

A ten-person open-source research lab cannot. Regulators write the rules, the biggest players help shape them, and everyone else disappears.

A bureaucratic caste backed by a handful of billionaires wealthy enough to buy themselves a seat at the table. That’s what a closed world looks like.

Europe has already gone down this road. The result? Models launch in the United States and China, while Europe gets them months later — if they arrive at all.

Meanwhile, as America prepares to shackle itself, China is rolling out open-source models one after another and making them available to the rest of the world.

Here’s my conclusion: The Huang scandal will be just the first pretext. Not the last. Every incident, every fear, every headline will be used to close another door.

If AI remains open, it belongs to everyone. If it becomes closed, it belongs to whoever controls the licenses. And on that day, it’s all over.
